summary: Describes DNSSEC Lookaside Validation (DLV), a way to publish DNSSEC trust anchors outside the normal DNS delegation chain. It helped resolvers validate zones whose parents were unsigned or did not publish DS records. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: DNSSEC proves that DNS data was signed by the zone it claims to come from, by following signatures up the tree of domain delegations to a trust anchor the resolver already holds. RFC 5074 adds a side door: a trusted domain can publish a statement saying another zone is signed, so the resolver does not need a built-in anchor for that zone.

questions: how does dlv name mapping work
subtitle: A way to publish DNSSEC trust anchors outside the DNS delegation chain, so validators need fewer built-in ones.

tldr.problem: A DNSSEC validator normally needs a trust anchor for every zone it wants to check, because the chain of signatures runs up the DNS delegation tree. With the root and many top level domains unsigned, that means a large list of built-in anchors in every resolver.
tldr.mechanism: DLV lets a separate domain publish trust statements about zones that are not its children. A validator that trusts the DLV domain finds a DLV record there and uses it in place of the DS record it would have needed from the zone's parent.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines how the DLV names are derived from the target zone, how a validator picks the closest enclosing record, and how aggressive negative caching cuts the load on the DLV servers. It is Historic today.

facts.label: Records a DLV domain needs
facts.value: DLV records, DNSSEC records, apex NS and SOA

today: RFC 5074 is Historic, so it is no longer a current standards document, and the unit metadata lists no replacement RFC for it. It was published in November 2007 as an Informational document describing how to publish DNSSEC trust anchors outside the delegation chain.

sections.title: Why Trust Anchors Outside the Delegation Chain
sections.content:
DNSSEC authenticates DNS data by building a chain of public key signatures along the DNS delegation chain, starting from a trust anchor. The trust anchor has to come from outside the DNS, because it is what makes the rest of the chain checkable.

In the world the RFC describes, the DNS root and many key top level domains are unsigned. That leaves a validating resolver with only one way to validate the many signed zones: keep a sizable collection of preconfigured trust anchors. Maintaining multiple preconfigured trust anchors in every DNSSEC-aware validator is a significant management challenge, and the work has to be repeated in each one.

The mechanism the RFC describes publishes trust anchors in the DNS outside the normal delegation chain. The stated aim is to make it easy to configure many validators within an organisation, or to let trust anchor management be done elsewhere on the organisation's behalf.
sections.plainLanguage: To check a signed domain, a resolver has to start from somewhere it already trusts and follow the signatures from there. Most of the top of the DNS tree is not signed, so the resolver needs a separate starting point for each signed domain it cares about, and those starting points have to be built in by hand.

sections.title: How DLV Adds a Third Path to Trust
sections.content:
DLV allows a set of domains, called DLV domains, to publish secure entry points for zones that are not their own children.

Under DNSSEC a validator may expect a zone to be secure when it holds one of two things: a preconfigured trust anchor for that zone, or a validated Delegation Signer record for the zone in the zone's parent, which in turn presumes a preconfigured trust anchor for the parent or some other ancestor. DLV adds a third mechanism: a validated entry in a DLV domain, which presumes a preconfigured trust anchor for the DLV domain. Whenever a DLV domain contains a DLV record set for a zone, a validator may expect the named zone to be signed.

The absence of a DLV record set for a zone does not necessarily mean the zone should be expected to be insecure. If the validator has another reason to believe the zone should be secured, validation of that zone's data should still be attempted.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a resolver trusts a signed domain because its parent says so, and the parent is trusted because of an ancestor. DLV gives a third route: a trusted domain elsewhere in DNS can vouch for it, so the resolver only needs a built-in anchor for that one trusted domain.

sections.title: DLV Domains and Name Mapping
sections.content:
A DLV domain holds trust statements about the descendants of a single zone, called the target zone. The DLV domain trustbroker.example.com could target the org zone, and the DLV domain bar.example.com could target the root.

The DLV domain contains one or more DLV records for each of the target's descendant zones that have registered security information with it. The name of the corresponding record is formed by replacing the target zone name with the DLV domain name. So, with trustbroker.example.com targeting the org zone, the DLV records for the zone example.org live at example.trustbroker.example.com, and the DLV records for the org zone live at the apex of trustbroker.example.com. With bar.example.com targeting the root, the records for example.org live at example.org.bar.example.com, the records for the org zone at org.bar.example.com, and the records for the root zone at the apex of bar.example.com.

A DLV domain need hold nothing else: DLV records, the DNSSEC records that validate them, the apex NS and SOA records, and optionally delegations. The RFC says the operator of a DLV domain will probably not want to include any other record types in it. To gain the full benefit of aggressive negative caching, a DLV domain SHOULD NOT use minimally-covering NSEC records as described in RFC 4470, and it SHOULD NOT use NSEC3 records.
sections.plainLanguage: The names inside a DLV domain are built by swapping the target zone's name for the DLV domain's name. If the DLV domain trusts the whole org zone, then the trust statement about example.org sits at example.org's name with the org part replaced.

sections.title: How a Validator Uses DLV
sections.content:
To keep the load on the DLV domain's servers and the query response time down, a validator SHOULD first try validation with any applicable trust anchor that is not a DLV one. If that succeeds, with a result of Secure, DLV processing need not happen at all. When it is configured with a trust anchor for a DLV domain, a validator SHOULD attempt to validate all responses at and below the target of that DLV domain.

To validate using DLV, the validator looks for a validated DLV record set that applies to the query and uses it as though it were a DS record set, following the normal procedures in Section 5 of RFC 4035. For each response it uses the closest enclosing DLV record set in the DLV domain, meaning the one with the longest name that matches the query or could be an ancestor of the query name. With trustbroker.example.com targeting org, and record sets named trustbroker.example.com for org, example.trustbroker.example.com for example.org and sub.example.trustbroker.example.com for sub.example.org, a validator answering a query for sub.example.org uses the sub.example.trustbroker.example.com record set.

Finding that record set starts with a lookup for the query name itself. If there is no record set for that name, confirmed by the presence of a validated NSEC record, and the name is not the apex of the DLV domain, the validator removes the leading label and tries again, repeating until it finds a record set or proves that none applies. In every case it SHOULD check its cache before issuing a query.

Whatever it finds, the validator MUST validate it with the normal procedures of RFC 4035, following any delegations inside the DLV domain with normal DNSSEC validation applied. If the DLV record set validates as Bogus it MUST NOT be used, and the result for the original response SHOULD be Bogus as well. If it validates as Insecure, meaning the DLV record sits in an unsecured part of the DLV domain, it MUST NOT be used and the original result SHOULD be Insecure as well. If it validates as Secure, the validator treats the DLV record set as though it were a DS record set for the applicable zone and validates the answer with it. To limit complexity, validators SHOULD NOT try to use DLV to validate data from another DLV domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The resolver looks for the trust statement that covers the name being asked about, using the longest matching one it can find. It then checks that statement the same way it would check any other signed data. If the check fails, the original answer is treated as untrustworthy too.

sections.title: Aggressive Negative Caching
sections.content:
DLV domains often hold few entries, so the RFC asks DLV validators to implement aggressive negative caching in order to keep the load on their authoritative servers down.

Ordinary cached negative responses are indexed by the query name, class, type and the setting of the CD bit, and only a query matching that key is answered from the cache. With aggressive negative caching the validator, before sending a query, also checks whether any cached and validated NSEC record denies the existence of the record being looked for. As a result it makes no query for any name covered by a cached and validated NSEC record, and when answering clients it synthesises a negative answer whenever it holds an applicable validated NSEC, unless the CD bit was set on the incoming query.

Implementing this means keeping an ordered structure of NSEC records so that covering ones can be found quickly, and only NSEC records from DLV domains need to be in it. The RFC also notes that some DLV validator implementations do not synthesise negative answers into outgoing responses at all; they use aggressive negative caching only when looking up DLV records during their own internal validation.

The optimisation in Section 8 works the other way round. When an authoritative server answers a query for a DLV record set, it SHOULD include in the Additional section of the response all the DLV record sets that could apply, that is, those applicable to the query name and to any of its ancestors, together with NSEC records proving that no other applicable DLV record set exists. Servers need only include record sets they know about, so record sets in sub-zones may be left out. Validators still look for the closest enclosing record set first, but if they are given data about other DLV record sets in the zone they MAY cache and use it, assuming it validates, which saves further trips to the DLV domain's servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Most lookups against a small trust-publishing domain find nothing. The RFC asks the resolver to remember which names definitely do not exist, using the signed records that prove absence, so it can answer such questions without asking the server again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Validators MUST NOT use a DLV record unless it has been successfully authenticated. Normally a validator holds a trust anchor for the DLV domain and uses DNSSEC to validate the data in it.

Aggressive negative caching raises the need for basic validation of incoming NSEC records before they are cached. In particular the next name field in an NSEC record MUST be within the zone that generated and signed it. Otherwise a malicious zone operator could generate an NSEC that reaches out of its zone, into its ancestor zones and even up to the root, and use it to spoof away any name that sorts after the NSEC's own name. The RFC calls these overreaching NSECs. More insidiously, an attacker could combine an overreaching NSEC with a signed wildcard record to substitute a signed positive answer for the real data. The check is not a new requirement, since these attacks are a risk even without aggressive negative caching, but caching makes it more important: before, an overreaching NSEC was cached only as metadata tied to a particular query, so one caused by a broken zone signing tool would only affect the queries it was fetched for, while now it can cause broader problems even with no attacker present. Checking the bounds of the NSEC removes the risk.

Validators MUST NOT use the mere presence of an RRSIG or an apex DNSKEY record set as a trigger to start validating, whether through the normal DNSSEC hierarchy or through DLV. An attacker could otherwise strip those records off and force a downgrade.

The RFC also notes that the security considerations specific to the DS record in Section 8 of RFC 4034 apply equally to DLV records. Of particular note, the key tag field helps pick the right DNSKEY record efficiently but does not identify one uniquely: two distinct DNSKEY records can share an owner name, an algorithm type and a key tag, so an implementation that selects a DNSKEY record using only the key tag may pick the wrong public key.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules keep this safe. A trust statement must be signed and checked before it is used. And a record that proves a name does not exist must not be allowed to claim names outside the zone that signed it, or a careless zone could hide real names behind it.

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS A VALIDATOR DECIDES A ZONE IS SECURE

items.title: Preconfigured trust anchor
items.text: The validator already holds a key for the zone itself.

items.title: Validated DS record
items.text: The zone's parent holds a signed DS record for it, and the parent is trusted in turn.

items.title: Validated DLV entry
items.text: A trusted DLV domain publishes a signed statement about the zone, and the validator treats that statement as if it were a DS record.

viz.caption: THE THREE DNSSEC VALIDATION RESULTS AND WHAT DLV DOES WITH THEM

items.label: Secure
items.desc: The DLV record set validated. The validator treats it as a DS record set and validates the answer with it.

items.label: Bogus
items.desc: The DLV record set failed validation. It must not be used, and the original answer should be Bogus too.

items.label: Insecure
items.desc: The DLV record sits in an unsecured part of the DLV domain. It must not be used, and the original answer should be Insecure too.
